title: Phase-Sensitive Validation of Reduced-Order Nonlinear Mechanical Models with Dynamic Readout
authors: Kazi T. Mahmood, M. Arif Hasan
abstract: Reduced-order models of nonlinear structures are often evaluated using mechanical response errors, while the signals of interest may also pass through dynamic readout channels that modify their amplitudes and phases. We develop an offline validation framework that distinguishes mechanical source error, readout-model prediction error, and physical distortion of a normalized two-component modal state. We couple a Galerkin reduced source to two calibrated resonant channels and evaluate modal amplitudes, relative phase, and state fidelity using consistent complex coefficients. For the linear readout model, an exact output-error decomposition distinguishes source and interface modeling contributions, while a two-channel identity relates differential channel transfer to normalized-state distortion. For the ten-mass nonlinear lattice, the two-mode source and coupled-output errors over the two-resonance interface band are $3.069 \times 10^{-2}$ and $2.448 \times 10^{-2}$. At $F_0=0.04$, the relative-phase mean absolute error increases from $9.82 \times 10^{-3}$ rad for the linear interface to $1.74 \times 10^{-2}$ rad for the nonlinear interface. At the strongest forcing, a four-coordinate proper orthogonal decomposition model gives a source error of $2.05 \times 10^{-2}$, compared with $8.03 \times 10^{-2}$ for four linear modes on the same held-out test set. The noise analysis shows that accurate in-band output prediction can coexist with substantial parameter error, while a constrained linear approximation of nonlinear readout data produces a substantial residual. We use these findings to assess reduced-model adequacy for the specified outputs, forcing levels, and validation frequencies.
summary: This work presents a comprehensive validation framework for reduced-order models of nonlinear mechanical systems. It distinguishes between errors originating in the mechanical source, the readout channel model, and the resulting physical state distortion. The findings provide quantitative metrics for assessing model adequacy, which is crucial for reliable data interpretation in complex physical measurements.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately validating reduced-order models (ROMs) for nonlinear mechanical structures when the measured signals pass through complex, dynamic readout channels.
main_result: The developed framework successfully separates and quantifies errors arising from the mechanical source, the readout model prediction, and the physical distortion of the modal state.
method: It employs an offline validation framework using consistent complex coefficients to analyze modal amplitudes, relative phases, and state fidelity across different interface models (linear vs. nonlinear).
model_or_system: The system is a nonlinear mechanical lattice whose dynamics are modeled by a full-order equation, which is then reduced via Galerkin projection. The output is coupled to a dynamic readout subsystem.
key_observables: Source error ($E_{src}$), readout prediction error ($E_{out}$), relative-phase mean absolute error ($E_{\phi,MAE}$), and normalized-state fidelity ($F_\psi$).
important_parameters: Forcing levels ($F_0$), resonance frequencies ($\omega_{o,j}$), and coupling parameters ($\eta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to separate source, readout, and state distortion effects, though it notes that constrained linear approximations may not reflect the true physical behavior.
figures_summary: Figures summarize the source-to-output modeling pipeline and error metrics, comparing results for linear versus cubic nonlinear interfaces, particularly showing increased phase and state errors with cubic distortion.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the full nonlinear source model, details the coupled dynamic readout interface, develops the validation framework using complex coefficients, and presents quantitative comparisons of errors across different forcing and interface conditions.
why_interesting: While focused on mechanics, the rigorous methodology for decomposing total error into distinct physical sources (source vs. measurement/readout) is highly relevant to open quantum systems where measurement back-action and readout fidelity are critical concerns.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Source-to-output modeling and validation. Galerkin reduction deﬁnes the source ROM, and calibration determines the interface parameters. The source-state block retains the modal signals qj(t) that drive the interface; the normalized state ψsrc is used for state comparisons. The validation metrics assess source accuracy, output prediction, and physical state preservation.

Figure 2a compares the mass-7 displacement response of the full-order model with reduced responses retaining r = 1, 2, 3, 4 modes at F0 = 0.04. Four linear natural frequencies lie within the 0.20–1.20 rad/s band. The one-mode model represents the lowest-frequency response, and the additional modes improve representation of the remaining resonances. Diﬀerences from the full response in- clude contributions from omitted modes and nonlinear interactions not resolved within each selected subspace.
Figure 2: Source-ROM order study at F0 = 0.04 over 0.20–1.20 rad/s. Panel 2a shows full-order and reduced responses for r = 1, 2, 3, 4. Panel 2b shows source band error and phase RMS error.
Figure 3: Dependence of source, output, and normalized-state errors on retained order and forcing amplitude over 0.20–0.66 rad/s. Each cell uses independently converged full and reduced responses.

Figure 4: Physical source-to-output transfer after static gain calibration and common-delay correc- tion. Panel 4a shows the relative-phase residual retaining the dynamic transducer phase. Panel 4b shows the state error 1−Fψ on a logarithmic scale. Cubic interface distortion increases both errors.
